_about: Question-specific grading criteria and follow-ups, keyed by question id. Overrides the generic defaults from the export script. Each criterion is one checkable thing a strong answer contains. See .agents/skills/interview-question/SKILL.md.

criteria: Names the 28-point train/validation gap as high variance (overfitting)
Proposes constraining the tree: max_depth, min_samples_leaf or pruning
Mentions averaging trees (random forest) as an alternative
Says what to check if the gap persists: leakage, label noise or a shifted validation set
classical-ml-questions:cml-high-variance.followup: You limit depth and validation stays at 71%. What do you look at next?

criteria: Identifies low, close train and validation scores as high bias (underfitting)
Uses the 95% human score as the reference for how much is achievable
Proposes more capacity, better features, less regularisation or longer training
Explains why collecting more data will not fix underfitting
classical-ml-questions:cml-high-bias.followup: How would you know you had fixed bias and not just moved to overfitting?

criteria: Computes 10,000 × 4/5 = 8,000 training rows per model
Notes each row is used for validation exactly once across the five runs
classical-ml-questions:cml-kfold-rows.followup: When is k-fold cross-validation the wrong choice?

criteria: Explains that random folds put future days in training (temporal leakage)
Proposes a time-based split: train before a cut-off, test after
Mentions a rolling or expanding window for repeated evaluation
States the principle: validation must mimic how the model is used in production
classical-ml-questions:cml-time-series-s.followup: How large a gap would you leave between the training cut-off and the test window, and why?

criteria: Asks whether the value is known at prediction time
Recognises account_closure_reason is written when the outcome happens (target leakage)
Removes the feature and anything derived from it
Expects AUC to drop to a believable number and treats 0.99 as a warning sign
classical-ml-questions:cml-leaky-feature.followup: How would you catch this kind of leak automatically before training?

criteria: Explains SMOTE interpolates between real minority points
Identifies that resampling before the split leaks near-copies of test rows into training
Fixes it: split first, resample only the training data, inside a pipeline per CV fold
Questions whether resampling is needed at all versus class weights and threshold tuning
classical-ml-questions:cml-smote-before-.followup: Do you need resampling at all here?

criteria: Computes precision = 15 / 50 = 0.3
Interprets it: 30% of flagged transactions are fraud
Names who bears the cost of low precision (the review team)
classical-ml-questions:cml-precision.followup: Who in the business cares most about precision here, and why?

criteria: Computes recall = 15 / 20 = 0.75
Interprets it: the model catches three quarters of the fraud
Explains that lowering the threshold raises recall and usually lowers precision
classical-ml-questions:cml-recall.followup: How would you raise recall, and what does it cost?

criteria: Explains the harmonic mean is pulled towards the lower of precision and recall
Names a case where F1 is the wrong metric (unequal error costs)
classical-ml-questions:cml-f1.followup: When would you not use F1 to choose between two models?

criteria: Explains 99% accuracy is what always predicting 'not fraud' scores
Recommends precision and recall at the operating threshold
Recommends PR-AUC for comparing models on the rare class
Explains why ROC-AUC can look optimistic under heavy imbalance
classical-ml-questions:cml-accuracy-imba.followup: Why can ROC-AUC look good while the model is useless for the rare class?

criteria: Works through a concrete population (e.g. 100,000 people: 100 sick, 99 true positives, 999 false positives)
Computes the positive predictive value ≈ 99 / 1,098 ≈ 0.09
Explains that a rare condition makes even an accurate test mostly produce false positives
Connects it to Bayes' rule or the base rate
classical-ml-questions:cml-base-rate.followup: How would you change the screening process to make a positive result more trustworthy?

criteria: Lets the review capacity (200 cases a day) set the threshold: rank and take the top k
Evaluates with precision@k
Compares the cost of missed fraud with the cost of a review
Mentions revisiting the threshold as fraud volume or model scores drift
classical-ml-questions:cml-threshold-cap.followup: Fraud volume doubles next month. What changes in your threshold policy?

criteria: Distinguishes ranking quality (AUC) from probability accuracy (calibration)
Checks a reliability diagram or Brier score
Fixes miscalibration with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data
Explains why prices need calibrated probabilities, not just a good ranking
classical-ml-questions:cml-calibration.followup: Which would you pick, Platt scaling or isotonic regression, with 2,000 validation examples?

criteria: Computes −ln(0.9) ≈ 0.105
Contrasts it with a confident miss: −ln(0.1) ≈ 2.30
Explains log loss punishes confident wrong predictions heavily
classical-ml-questions:cml-log-loss.followup: Why might a team choose log loss over accuracy when training and comparing models?

criteria: Chooses L1 regularisation because it can set many weights exactly to zero
Explains that the corners of the L1 penalty make the optimum land on feature axes
Proposes elastic net when important features are correlated
Explains that plain lasso may select one correlated feature arbitrarily
classical-ml-questions:cml-l1-sparse.followup: Why does L1 give exact zeros and L2 doesn't?

criteria: Names tree-based models as insensitive to feature scale
Explains that a tree split compares values only within one feature
Identifies distance-, dot-product-, and weight-penalty-based models as needing standardisation
Proposes a robust scaler or log transform when income has heavy outliers or skew
classical-ml-questions:cml-scaling.followup: When would you use standardisation instead of min-max scaling?

criteria: Rejects the built-in ranking as sufficient evidence because impurity importance favours high-cardinality features
Proposes permutation importance on held-out data
Explains that permutation importance measures the validation loss caused by shuffling the feature
Proposes out-of-fold target encoding or grouping zip codes into regions if the signal persists
classical-ml-questions:cml-impurity-impo.followup: What's the risk with target-encoding zip code?

criteria: Names the curse of dimensionality as the reason nearest neighbours become unreliable
Explains that nearest and farthest distances converge as irrelevant dimensions add noise
Proposes feature selection, PCA, or metric learning
Suggests a feature-weighting model such as boosted trees as an alternative
classical-ml-questions:cml-knn-dimension.followup: Why does PCA help, and when would it fail?

criteria: Names multicollinearity as the cause of unstable coefficient signs
Explains that many weight combinations fit equally well when features carry nearly the same information
Proposes dropping or combining a feature, or using ridge regression
Names variance inflation factor as a direct diagnostic
Identifies the income values as not missing at random
Explains that missingness itself carries default-risk signal
Proposes imputation plus a missing-value indicator
Notes that boosted trees can learn a branch direction for missing values
classical-ml-questions:cml-missing-infor.followup: Why should imputation happen inside each cross-validation fold?

criteria: Proposes monitoring feature distributions with measures such as PSI or KS tests
Proposes monitoring prediction distributions and missing or out-of-range values
Explains that drift is an investigation signal rather than proof of performance loss
Commits to computing outcome metrics when the delayed labels arrive
Classifies 0.678 as a large shift using the stated 0.25 rule of thumb
Explains that PSI depends on bucket choices and should be paired with performance metrics once labels arrive
Computes the pooled rate 0.105, standard error 0.00613, and z-score 0.01 / 0.00613 = 1.63
Concludes that 1.63 is below 1.96 and is not significant at the two-sided 5% level
Explains that the one-percentage-point lift needs more users before it is trusted
classical-ml-questions:cml-ab-z.followup: Can you just run the test longer until it's significant?

criteria: Explains that repeatedly checking and stopping at p < 0.05 inflates the false-positive rate
States that a conventional p-value assumes a preselected sample size and one analysis
Proposes either a fixed sample size or a monitoring-safe method such as group-sequential boundaries
Names always-valid sequential p-values as another valid option
classical-ml-questions:cml-ab-peeking.followup: What else can invalidate an A/B test?

criteria: Computes the initial cross-entropy as −ln(1/10) = ln(10) = 2.303
Explains that uniform predictions assign probability 1/10 to each class
Diagnoses a much higher first loss as oversized initial logits and a much lower loss as possible label leakage
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-init.followup: The first loss is 40. What's wrong?

criteria: Interprets loss stuck at ln(10) as outputs remaining uniform
Proposes overfitting one batch as the first debugging test
Names a broken gradient or optimiser path such as a missing optimizer.step() as a likely cause
Explains that the one-batch test separates implementation failure from a hard learning problem
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-flat.followup: It overfits one batch but not the full data. Now what?

criteria: Names the diverging train and validation losses as overfitting to training-set noise
Proposes stopping at the best validation epoch
Proposes reducing the gap with regularisation, augmentation, a smaller model, or more data
Explains that rising loss with improving accuracy can mean increasingly confident mistakes
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-val-.followup: Validation accuracy still improves while validation loss rises. How?

criteria: Identifies an excessively high learning rate as the primary cause
Proposes lowering the learning rate and adding warmup
Distinguishes a tiny batch by noting its noisy loss should still trend down on average
Proposes a learning-rate range test to locate where loss begins to diverge
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-osci.followup: How would a batch that's too small look different?

criteria: Explains that fp16 activation or gradient overflow produces infinity and then NaN
Proposes bf16 first when the hardware supports it
Proposes dynamic loss scaling, gradient clipping, or a lower learning rate for fp16
Names unstable unclamped softmax or logarithm operations as another place to inspect
Identifies the missing model.eval() call
Explains that dropout remains random and batch norm uses current-batch statistics in training mode
Proposes torch.no_grad() to reduce evaluation memory
Restores model.train() before training resumes
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-eval.followup: What does batch norm do differently in eval mode?

criteria: Explains that warmup limits badly directed early updates before Adam's moment estimates settle
Notes that warmup is especially useful for transformers trained with large learning rates
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-warm.followup: Why does Adam need warmup at all?

criteria: Computes cos(π/2) = 0 and lr = 0.5 × 3e-4 = 1.5e-04
States that cosine decay falls slowly at the start and end and fastest in the middle
Explains that smaller late-stage steps help the model settle instead of bouncing around a minimum
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-cosi.followup: Why decay the learning rate at all?

criteria: Explains that Adam rescales an L2 gradient with its adaptive denominator
Explains that AdamW applies lr × weight_decay × w separately from the adaptive update
Concludes that decoupling makes regularisation behave like true weight decay
Notes that biases and normalisation weights are usually excluded from decay
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-adam.followup: What weight decay is typical for transformers?

criteria: Applies the SGD linear-scaling rule by multiplying the learning rate by 4
Pairs the larger learning rate with warmup
Distinguishes Adam-style optimisation by naming square-root scaling as a common heuristic
Treats either rule as a starting point to validate with a short sweep
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-batc.followup: When does linear scaling stop working?

criteria: Attributes intermittent spikes to rare batches producing very large gradients
Proposes clipping the global gradient norm
Explains that norm clipping preserves gradient direction while bounding the step
Suggests lowering the learning rate or inspecting bad batches and Adam settings if spikes persist
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-grad.followup: Would you clip by value or by norm?

criteria: Computes std = sqrt(2/512) = 0.0625
Explains that the factor of 2 compensates for ReLU zeroing about half its inputs
Connects the scale to keeping activation variance roughly constant across layers
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-he-i.followup: What happens with standard deviation 0.01 in a 50-layer ReLU network?

criteria: Explains that two-example batch statistics are too noisy for batch norm
Explains that noisy running statistics also create a train/evaluation mismatch
Proposes GroupNorm or LayerNorm because they normalise within each example
Proposes SyncBatchNorm when statistics can be aggregated across GPUs
Distinguishes worse training accuracy in the deeper model as degradation rather than overfitting
Proposes residual connections of the form x + f(x)
Explains that residual connections make the identity function easy to represent
Explains that the identity derivative gives gradients a direct path around the block
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-resi.followup: Why does x + f(x) help gradients?

criteria: Computes 4,096 × 4,096 weights + 4,096 biases = 16,781,312 parameters
Separates the 16,777,216 weights from the 4,096 biases
Connects large projection layers to most parameters in transformer attention and MLP blocks
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-line.followup: How many parameters are in the MLP of a block with hidden size 4,096 and a 4× expansion?

criteria: Computes 128 × (3 × 3 × 64 + 1) = 73,856 parameters
Explains that the image dimensions do not affect the parameter count
Explains that convolutional parameters are shared across spatial positions
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-conv.followup: What is the compute for a 56×56 output?

criteria: Computes 7 × 10^9 parameters × 2 bytes = 14 GB
States that bf16 uses two bytes per parameter
Distinguishes weight memory from additional KV-cache and activation memory
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-weig.followup: How much would the weights take in int4?

criteria: Computes 2 + 2 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes per parameter and 7 × 10^9 × 16 = 112 GB
Accounts for bf16 weights and gradients plus fp32 master weights and two Adam moments
Explains that the 112 GB excludes activations and motivates sharding or LoRA
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-adam.followup: What does ZeRO stage 3 or FSDP do with this memory?

criteria: Proposes gradient accumulation to preserve an effective batch of 32 with smaller micro-batches
Explains that several forward/backward passes precede one optimizer.step()
Notes the batch-normalisation exception to mathematical equivalence
Proposes activation checkpointing or mixed precision for additional memory savings
Computes effective batch = 8 × 16 × 4 = 512
Identifies micro-batch size, accumulation steps, and data-parallel GPU count as the three factors
Uses the effective batch rather than the micro-batch when reasoning about learning rate
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-effe.followup: You move to 8 GPUs and want the same effective batch. What changes?

criteria: Computes throughput = 8 × 50,000 = 400,000 tokens/s and time = 10^9 / 400,000 = 2,500 seconds = 41.7 minutes
States that the arithmetic ignores data loading, evaluation, checkpointing, and communication
Adds a 20–40% planning margin for those overheads
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-trai.followup: Would scaling from 8 to 64 GPUs make the run exactly 8× faster?

criteria: Chooses bf16 because its 8-bit exponent gives it the same numeric range as fp32
Contrasts bf16's 7 mantissa bits with fp16's greater precision but narrow range
Explains that training is more sensitive to overflow and underflow than reduced precision
Explains that bf16 generally avoids dynamic loss scaling
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-bf16.followup: Where does bf16's low precision hurt?

criteria: Identifies augmented near-duplicates across splits as leakage
Proposes splitting by original-image group before augmentation
Restricts augmentation to the training split, preferably on the fly
Proposes perceptual hashes or embedding similarity to detect cross-split near-duplicates
deep-learning-training-questions:dl-augm.followup: What other kinds of groups can leak across a split like this?

criteria: Identifies single-sequence decode as memory-bandwidth-bound
Explains that every generated token streams the model weights for relatively few operations
Contrasts decode with compute-bound parallel prefill
Explains that batching reuses one weight read across multiple sequences
Computes 2 × 10^12 bytes/s / (14 × 10^9 bytes) = 143 tokens/s
Explains that the estimate assumes every weight is read once per token
Notes that KV-cache reads and sub-peak kernel bandwidth make real throughput lower
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: What happens to this ceiling with a batch of 32?

criteria: Identifies the ceiling as four times the bf16 result because int4 moves one quarter of the weight bytes
Explains that on-the-fly dequantisation and quality loss can reduce the practical benefit
Computes 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token
Accounts for both keys and values at every layer and KV head
Explains that grouped-query attention cuts this cache by 4× relative to 32 KV heads
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: Why doesn't the number of query heads appear?

criteria: Computes 8,192 × 128 KiB = 1,048,576 KiB = 1 GiB per sequence
Connects long-context serving cost to KV-cache growth
Distinguishes the per-sequence cache from the model's fixed weight memory
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: How much KV cache would a 128k-token context need?

criteria: Computes 40 GiB / 1 GiB per sequence = 40 concurrent sequences
Identifies KV-cache capacity as the concurrency limit after weights are loaded
Explains that paged attention avoids reserving a maximum-length cache for sequences that stay short
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: How else can you fit more concurrent sequences?

criteria: Explains that grouped-query attention shares one key-value head across several query heads
Connects fewer KV heads to proportionally smaller cache and decode bandwidth
Distinguishes multi-query attention as the one-KV-head extreme
Notes that the more aggressive multi-query design can cost more quality
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: Can you convert a multi-head model to grouped-query attention?

criteria: Explains that static batching leaves finished request slots idle until the longest response ends
Explains that continuous batching evicts finished sequences and inserts new requests at each decode step
Connects continuous batching and paged KV caches to higher GPU throughput
Names scheduling complexity and prefill/decode contention as costs
Identifies time to first token as the degraded metric
Separates TTFT into queueing and prompt prefill
Proposes prefix caching, context trimming, chunked prefill, or additional capacity
Separates TTFT reporting from time per output token because they have different causes
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: How would you measure where TTFT goes?

criteria: Chooses prefix caching for the shared 3,000-token system prompt
Explains that cached KV blocks avoid repeating prefill for identical tokens
Places stable prompt content before variable content to maximise the reusable prefix
Explains that an early changing token invalidates the cache for all later tokens
Computes (1 − 0.8^5) / (1 − 0.8) = 3.36 tokens per large-model pass
Includes the large model's guaranteed correction or continuation token in the expectation
Explains that memory-bound verification of four tokens costs roughly one ordinary decode pass
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: When does speculative decoding not help?

criteria: Explains that temperature zero still depends on tiny logit differences
Connects those differences to batch-dependent kernel choice and reduction order
Explains that nearly tied tokens can flip and make the remaining generation diverge
Names batch-invariant kernels as a deterministic but slower option
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:sr.followup: Why does nondeterminism at temperature zero matter for evaluation?

criteria: Chooses retrieval-augmented generation for a policy manual that changes weekly
Explains that retrieval keeps knowledge current and supports citations
Distinguishes fine-tuning as a tool for behaviour, format, tone, or task skill
Proposes combining light fine-tuning with retrieval when both behaviour and current facts matter
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: When would you fine-tune this support bot as well?

criteria: Defines the LoRA update as W + (α/r)BA with low-rank A and B matrices
Explains that only A and B receive gradients and optimiser state
Connects the low-rank trainable matrices to smaller memory use and checkpoints
Explains that adapters can be merged for zero extra inference cost or swapped per customer
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: Which model matrices do people usually adapt with LoRA?

criteria: Computes 4,096 × 16 + 16 × 4,096 = 131,072 trainable parameters
Contrasts the adapter with the original matrix's 16,777,216 parameters
Explains that the two trainable matrices have shapes 4,096 × 16 and 16 × 4,096
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: Why can such a small adapter work?

criteria: Places the result within the stated 0.1–1% typical whole-model range
Explains that optimiser-state memory shrinks with the trainable parameter count
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: Does training fewer parameters mean worse results?

criteria: Explains that QLoRA stores frozen base weights in 4-bit NormalFloat
Explains that base weights are dequantised during the forward pass while bf16 LoRA adapters receive gradients
Names paged optimisers as the mechanism for handling memory spikes
Contrasts the 7B base-weight footprint of about 3.5 GB with 14 GB in bf16
Computes 10,000 × 1,500 × 3 = 45,000,000 = 45 million training tokens
Connects token count to hosted fine-tuning cost
Explains that dividing tokens by processing throughput estimates training time
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: Is three epochs a good default for this dataset?

criteria: Names catastrophic forgetting from training only on a narrow legal distribution
Proposes replaying 10–30% general instruction data
Proposes a smaller learning rate, fewer epochs, or LoRA to reduce general-capability damage
Requires a fixed general-task evaluation alongside the legal-task evaluation before shipping
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: How would you detect this regression before launch?

criteria: Explains that teacher-forced validation always supplies the correct previous token
Explains that inference compounds errors from the model's own generated tokens
Notes that lower loss can reflect copying reference phrasing without better task performance
Chooses checkpoints using generated-output evaluation on held-out prompts
Checks for a mismatch between training and serving chat templates first
Names role markers, special tokens, and the end-of-turn token as format-critical
Explains that a missing stop token makes the model unable to recognise the end of its turn
Uses the tokenizer's template in both paths and tests the served endpoint with a training prompt
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: What makes the model stop generating?

criteria: Explains that PPO-based RLHF trains a reward model and then optimises a policy with reinforcement learning and a KL penalty
Explains that DPO directly raises preferred-answer likelihood relative to rejected answers and a reference model
Identifies DPO as simpler and more stable than the PPO pipeline
Names preference overfitting, length drift, or style drift as risks controlled partly by beta
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: What can go wrong with DPO?

criteria: Chooses the 1,000 expert-written examples for teaching instruction-following style

Explains that noisy examples teach inconsistent behaviour and errors
Distinguishes a genuinely new skill as a case that needs more data while retaining quality
llm-serving-and-fine-tuning-questions:ft.followup: How would you clean the 100,000 scraped examples?

criteria: Defines a foundation model as a large model pretrained at scale on broad data
Explains that one foundation model can adapt to many downstream tasks
Contrasts adaptation by prompting or fine-tuning with training a separate model from scratch per task
qa-quick-reference:0686ffdebb6f.followup: When would you still train a task-specific model instead?

criteria: Defines an LLM as a neural network, usually a decoder-only Transformer
States that pretraining predicts the next token from preceding tokens
Explains that chat, code, and reasoning behaviour emerge from scale and post-training on top of that objective

criteria: Defines tokenization as mapping text into a fixed vocabulary of subword units

Explains that whole-word tokenization needs an unbounded vocabulary and cannot handle unseen words
qa-quick-reference:a90852b31b07.followup: How does tokenization affect context length and inference cost?

criteria: Explains that BPE builds a vocabulary by repeatedly merging frequent adjacent byte or character pairs
States that the rare word falls back to several smaller subword pieces
Distinguishes rare-word splitting from the single-token representation common words may receive

criteria: Defines embeddings as dense numeric vectors for tokens, sentences, or documents
Explains that semantic similarity maps to geometric closeness
Connects embeddings to the representations consumed by attention and retrieval
qa-quick-reference:cfeb2ec2bf65.followup: How would you test whether an embedding model captures similarity for your domain?

criteria: States that the encoder would treat the two token orderings equivalently without positional information
Explains that self-attention alone is permutation-invariant
Explains that positional encoding injects token order so the meanings can differ

Connects attention weights to the relevance of other positions
qa-quick-reference:90e4b1c73699.followup: What is the computational cost of full self-attention as sequence length grows?

criteria: Defines Query as what the current position seeks
Defines Key as what each position offers
Explains that Query-Key similarity produces weights used to combine Values

criteria: Explains that unscaled dot products grow with key dimension
Explains that large scores saturate softmax toward one-hot weights and near-zero gradients
Explains that division by sqrt(d_k) keeps scores in a trainable range

criteria: Defines multi-head attention as parallel smaller attention computations with separate projections

Explains that separate heads can specialise in different relationships instead of averaging them into one head

criteria: States that decoder cross-attention queries come from the decoder
States that keys and values come from the encoder output

Explains that generation fails because future tokens do not exist at inference time

criteria: Computes 2 × 24 × 16 × 64 × 2 = 98,304 bytes = 96 KiB per token
Accounts for keys and values across every layer and KV head
Explains that caching avoids recomputing all prior token projections during each decode step

criteria: Chooses retrieval for the daily-changing price list

Explains that fine-tuning is slow to update and does not reliably cite current sources

criteria: Describes chunking source documents and embedding each chunk
Describes indexing embeddings and embedding the incoming query
Describes retrieving nearest chunks and supplying them with the query as LLM context

Explains that rank-only fusion works when cosine and BM25 scores are not directly comparable

Explains that graph traversal can connect facts a single chunk-similarity search will not

criteria: Chooses faithfulness as the metric for unsupported answer claims
